blocks.p: And now Mr. Sagacity left me to dream out my dream by myself. So it seemed to me that I saw Christiana and Mercy and the boys all go up to the gate; and when they got there, they held a short debate about how they should manage their calling at the gate, and what should be said to the One who opened to them. It was decided that since Christiana was the eldest, she should knock for entrance, and speak for the rest to the One who opened.

So Christiana began to knock; and like her poor husband before her, she knocked, and knocked again. But instead of any answer, they all thought they heard a dog come barking at them, and a great one too; and this made the women and children afraid, so that for a while they dared not knock any more, for fear the mastiff would fly at them. Now they were greatly tossed about in their minds and did not know what to do. Knock they dared not, for fear of the dog; go back they dared not, for fear the Keeper of the gate should see them going and be offended. At last they thought of knocking again, and knocked harder than they had at first.
“Who is there?” said the Keeper of the gate. Then the dog stopped barking, and he opened to them.
Christiana bowed low, and said, “Let not our Lord be offended with his handmaids for knocking at his princely gate.”
“Where do you come from,” said the Keeper, “and what is it you want?”

“We have come from where Christian came from, and on the same errand as his: to be, if it pleases you, graciously admitted by this gate into the way that leads to the Celestial City. And I answer, my Lord, in the next place, that I am Christiana, once the wife of Christian, who has now gotten above.”
At that the Keeper of the gate marveled. “What!” he said. “Has she become a pilgrim now, who only a while ago abhorred that life?”
She bowed her head and said, “Yes; and so have these my sweet babes.”

Then he took her by the hand and led her in, saying, “Let the little children come to me”; and with that he shut the gate. This done, he called to a trumpeter above the gate to welcome Christiana with shouting and the sound of the trumpet for joy. So the trumpeter sounded, and filled the air with his melodious notes. [Luke 15:7]

Now all this while poor Mercy stood outside, trembling and crying, for fear that she was rejected. But when Christiana had gained admittance for herself and her boys, she began to intercede for Mercy.

“My Lord,” she said, “I have a companion who is still standing outside, who has come here on the same account as myself. She is much cast down in her mind, because she comes, as she thinks, without being sent for; whereas I was sent for by my husband’s King.”

Now Mercy had begun to grow very impatient, for every minute was as long as an hour to her; so she cut short Christiana’s intercession by knocking at the gate herself. And she knocked so loud that she made Christiana start.
“Who is there?” said the Keeper of the gate.
“It is my friend,” said Christiana.
So he opened the gate and looked out; but Mercy had fallen down outside in a swoon, for she had fainted, afraid that no gate would be opened to her.
Then he took her by the hand and said, “Young woman, I bid you rise.”
“Oh, sir,” she said, “I am faint; there is scarcely any life left in me.”

“Someone once said,” he answered, “’When my soul fainted within me, I remembered the Lord; and my prayer came in to you, into your holy temple.’ [Jonah 2:7] Do not be afraid, but stand on your feet, and tell me why you have come.”
“I have come for something I was never invited to, as my friend Christiana was. Her invitation was from the King; mine was only from her. So I am afraid I presume.”
“Did she ask you to come with her to this place?”
“Yes; and, as my Lord sees, I have come. And if there is any grace or forgiveness of sins to spare, I beg that I, your poor handmaid, may have a share of it.”

Then he took her again by the hand, and led her gently in, and said, “I pray for all who believe in me, by whatever means they come to me.” Then he said to those who stood by, “Fetch something and give it to Mercy to smell, to stop her fainting.” So they fetched her a bundle of myrrh, and after a while she revived.

And now Christiana and her boys, and Mercy, were received by the Lord at the head of the way, and spoken to kindly by him. Then they said to him further, “We are sorry for our sins, and beg our Lord’s pardon, and further instruction as to what we must do.”

“I grant pardon,” he said, “by word and by deed: by word, in the promise of forgiveness; by deed, in the way I obtained it. Take the first from my lips with a kiss [Song 1:2], and the other as it shall be revealed.” [John 20:20]

Now I saw in my dream that he spoke many good words to them, which made them very glad. He also took them up to the top of the gate, and showed them by what deed they were saved; and he told them that they would have that sight again as they went along the way, for their comfort.
Then he left them for a while in a summer parlor below, where they fell to talking among themselves. Christiana began: “Oh, Lord, how glad I am that we have gotten in here!”
“So you well may be,” said Mercy, “but I of all have cause to leap for joy.”
“At one point, as I stood at the gate, because I had knocked and no one answered, I thought all our labor was lost, especially when that ugly cur made such a heavy barking at us.”

“But my worst fear came after I saw that you were taken into his favor, and I was left behind. Now, I thought, it is fulfilled which is written: ‘Two women shall be grinding together; the one shall be taken, and the other left.’ [Matt. 24:41] I could hardly keep from crying out, ‘Undone! Undone!’ And I was afraid to knock any more. But when I looked up at what was written over the gate, I took courage. I thought too that I must either knock again or die; so I knocked, but I cannot tell you how, for my spirit was struggling then between life and death.”

“You cannot tell how you knocked? I am sure your knocks were so earnest that the very sound of them made me start. I thought I had never heard such knocking in all my life. I thought you would have come in by violent hands, or taken the kingdom by storm.” [Matt. 11:12]

“Alas, who in my case could have done otherwise? You saw that the door was shut on me, and that there was a most cruel dog about. Who that was as faint-hearted as I, I ask you, would not have knocked with all their might? But tell me, what did my Lord say to my rudeness? Was he not angry with me?”

“When he heard your thunderous noise, he gave a wonderfully innocent smile. I believe what you did pleased him well enough, for he showed no sign to the contrary. But I marvel in my heart why he keeps such a dog. If I had known that before, I am afraid I should not have had the heart to venture here like this. But now we are in, we are in; and I am glad with all my heart.”
“Next time he comes down, if you like, I will ask him why he keeps such a filthy cur in his yard. I hope he will not take it amiss.”
“Yes, do,” said the children, “and persuade him to hang it; for we are afraid it will bite us when we leave.”
So at last he came down to them again, and Mercy fell on her face before him, and worshiped, and said, “Let my Lord accept the sacrifice of praise which I now offer him with the calves of my lips.”
“Peace be to you,” he said. “Stand up.”

But she stayed on her face, and said, “’Righteous are you, O Lord, when I plead with you; yet let me talk with you of your judgments.’ [Jer. 12:1] Why do you keep so cruel a dog in your yard, when the sight of it makes such women and children as we are ready to flee from your gate in fear?”

“That dog has another owner,” he answered. “He is kept, too, on another man’s ground; only my pilgrims hear his barking. He belongs to the castle you see there in the distance, but he can come up to the walls of this place. He has frightened many an honest pilgrim from worse to better by the great voice of his roaring. Indeed, the one who owns him does not keep him out of any good will to me or mine, but with the intent of keeping pilgrims from coming to me, so that they will be afraid to knock at this gate for entrance. Sometimes he has broken out and savaged some that I loved; but for the present I bear it all patiently. I also give my pilgrims timely help, so that they are not delivered up to his power, to be done to as his doggish nature would prompt him. But what! my purchased one, I think that if you had known ever so much beforehand, you would not have been afraid of a dog.

“Beggars who go from door to door will, rather than lose a hoped-for alms, run the risk of the bawling, barking, and biting too of a dog; and shall a dog, a dog in another man’s yard, a dog whose barking I turn to the profit of pilgrims, keep anyone from coming to me? I deliver them from the lions, and their darling from the power of the dog.”
“I confess my ignorance,” said Mercy. “I spoke of what I did not understand. I acknowledge that you do all things well.”

Then Christiana began to talk of their journey, and to inquire about the way. So he fed them, and washed their feet, and set them in the way of his steps, as he had dealt with her husband before. And I saw in my dream that they walked on in their way, and the weather was very pleasant for them.
Then Christiana began to sing:

v: Blessed be the day that I began
and blessed also be the man
who turned my heart that day.
It’s true, it was a long time till
but now I run with all my will:
Our tears to joy, our fears to faith,
are turned, as we can see;
so our beginning, as one says,
shows what our end will be.

blocks.p: Now on the other side of the wall that fenced in the way Christiana and her companions were to travel, there was a garden; and that garden belonged to the owner of the barking dog mentioned before. Some of the fruit trees that grew in that garden shot their branches over the wall, and the fruit, being ripe, was picked up by those who found it, and often eaten to their hurt. So Christiana’s boys, as boys will, pleased with the trees and the fruit hanging on them, pulled at the branches and began to eat. Their mother scolded them for it, but still the boys went on.

“Well, my sons,” she said, “you are in the wrong, for that fruit is not ours.” But she did not know that it belonged to the enemy; I warrant you, if she had, she would have been ready to die for fear. But that passed, and they went on their way.

Now when they had gone about two bowshots from the place that let them into the way, they saw two very ill-favored men coming quickly down the road to meet them. At that, Christiana and her friend Mercy covered themselves with their veils and kept on their journey; the children went on ahead; and so at last they all met. The two who had come down to meet them came right up to the women as if to embrace them.
“Stand back,” said Christiana, “or go peaceably by, as you should.”

But the two, like deaf men, paid no attention to Christiana’s words, and began to lay hands on them. At that Christiana, growing very angry, kicked out at them with her feet. Mercy too, as well as she could, did what she could to shake them off.
“Stand back and be gone,” said Christiana again, “for we have no money to lose. We are pilgrims, as you see, and live on the charity of our friends.”
“We make no assault on you for money,” said one of the two. “We have come out to tell you that if you will only grant one small request we shall ask, we will make women of you forever.”

Now Christiana, guessing what they meant, answered, “We will neither hear, nor regard, nor yield to what you ask. We are in haste and cannot stay; our business is a business of life and death.” So again she and her companions tried to push past them; but the men blocked their way.
“We intend no harm to your lives,” they said. “It is another thing we want.”

“Ah,” said Christiana, “you would have us body and soul, for I know that is what you have come for. But we will die on the spot rather than let ourselves be brought into snares that would ruin our well-being hereafter.” And with that they both shrieked out and cried, “Murder! Murder!” and so put themselves under the laws that are provided for the protection of women. [Deut. 22:23-27] But the men still pressed on them, meaning to have their way. So they cried out again.

Now since they were, as I said, not far from the gate they had come in at, their voices were heard from there; so some of the household came out, and recognizing Christiana’s voice, hurried to her relief. By the time they came within sight of them, the women were in a very great scuffle, and the children stood by crying. Then the one who had come to their relief called out to the ruffians, “What is this you are doing? Would you make my Lord’s people sin?” He tried to seize them too, but they made their escape over the wall into the garden of the man who owned the great dog; so the dog became their protector.

Then this Reliever came up to the women and asked how they were. “We thank your Prince,” they answered, “pretty well; only we have been somewhat frightened. We thank you too for coming to our help, for otherwise we would have been overcome.”

After a few more words, the Reliever said, “I marveled much, when you were received at the gate above, that you did not petition the Lord there for a guide, since you knew you were but weak women. Then you might have avoided these troubles and dangers, for he would have granted you one.”

“Alas,” said Christiana, “we were so taken up with our present blessing that dangers to come were forgotten by us. Besides, who could have thought that so near the King’s palace there should lurk such wicked men? Indeed, it would have been well for us if we had asked our Lord for one; but since our Lord knew it would be for our good, I wonder that he did not send one along with us!”

“It is not always necessary to grant things that are not asked for, lest by so doing they come to be little valued. But when the want of a thing is felt, then it comes to be valued, in the eyes of the one who feels it, at the worth that is properly its due, and so afterward is used accordingly. If my Lord had granted you a guide, you would not now be grieving over your oversight in not asking for one, as you have occasion to do. So all things work for good, and tend to make you more wary.”
“Shall we go back to my Lord, and confess our folly, and ask for one?”

“I will present your confession of your folly to him. You need not go back; for in every place you come to, you will find no want at all, since in every one of my Lord’s lodgings, which he has prepared for the reception of his pilgrims, there is enough to furnish them against every attack whatsoever. But, as I said, ‘He will be inquired of by them, to do it for them.’ [Ezek. 36:37] And it is a poor thing that is not worth asking for.” When he had said this, he went back to his place, and the pilgrims went on their way.
“What a sudden blow this is!” said Mercy. “I had made up my mind that we were past all danger now, and should never see sorrow again.”

“Your innocence, my sister,” said Christiana, “may excuse you a great deal; but as for me, my fault is so much the greater, for I saw this danger before I ever came out of doors, and yet did not provide for it where provision might have been had. I am much to blame.”
“How did you know this before you left home? Open this riddle to me.”

“Why, I will tell you. Before I set foot out of doors, one night as I lay in my bed, I had a dream about this. I seemed to see two men, as like these two as any in the world could look, standing at the foot of my bed, plotting how they might prevent my salvation. I will tell you their very words. They said (it was when I was in my troubles), ‘What shall we do with this woman? She cries out, waking and sleeping, for forgiveness. If she is allowed to go on as she has begun, we shall lose her as we lost her husband.’ This, you know, might have made me take heed, and provide while provision might have been had.”

“Well,” said Mercy, “as by this neglect we have been given an occasion to see our own imperfections, so our Lord has taken the occasion to make known the riches of his grace; for he, as we see, has followed us with unasked-for kindness, and has delivered us from the hands of those stronger than we, of his own good pleasure.”
